title: Pew finds 34% of US adults now use AI chatbots for health-related tasks
subtitle: A 3,488-respondent survey reports fast adoption for symptom checks and general information — but only 29% are very comfortable sharing personal health data with the tools.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Pew Research Center published a new survey on August 25, 2026 finding that 34% of US adults now use AI chatbots for at least one health-related task. The three most common uses are looking up quick health information (28%), understanding symptoms (25%), and accessing low-cost information (22%). Roughly 47% of users describe the answers as extremely or very helpful, but only 29% say they are very comfortable sharing personal health data with the tools. The survey was fielded June 22–28 with 3,488 US adults.

The data matters because it is the first large representative sample of consumer AI use in a specific high-stakes domain, and it lands during a policy push to define how chatbots may present health content. Asian American adults (56%) and adults under 30 (44%) show the highest adoption. A companion Pew report published the same day found Americans are more likely to say chatbots hurt than help people using them for loneliness, depression, or stress — a signal that public tolerance for AI in mental-health contexts is materially lower than in physical-health information lookup.

The Pew numbers slot into a broader ecosystem shift. The FDA has cleared more than 1,350 AI-enabled medical devices as of the PLOS analysis this month, DeepHealth's AI breast-ultrasound cleared in early August, and Insilico's rentosertib became the first fully AI-designed drug to enter Phase III. The chatbot layer is the consumer-facing edge of that same push, and it is now large enough that both providers and regulators have to design for it explicitly rather than around it.

For learners: the useful frame here is separating tasks from trust. People are willing to use chatbots for retrieval and framing — 'what could this symptom mean' — but not for anything requiring genuine data disclosure. If you are building anything in the healthcare-AI space, that split is a design constraint, not a marketing challenge. Ship the retrieval feature first, earn the trust separately, and never confuse a helpful answer with a clinically actionable one.
